question: Geological basins in Europe are still largely unexploited, though some Member States such as the Netherlands have already begun to produce heat from geothermal energy.

While these basins are unevenly distributed across the EU, the support given to geothermal energy by the resolution adopted in plenary on 18 January 2024 (P9_TA(2024)0049) should make it possible to embark on large-scale exploitation of this form of energy so as to boost our energy independence.

However, exploitation methods involve risks and still prompt opposition (reservoir depletion, seismicity, dealing with landowners, pollution). Yet the report adopted on in Strasbourg makes little mention of that. Accordingly: 1.
Does the Commission have a funding programme for geothermal research that factors in the risks concerned?

What measures does the Commission envisage so as to address concerns about public-private partnerships in the geothermal sector, while promoting the sustainable development of this energy source in Europe?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.3.2024) The European funding programme Horizon Europe1 addresses environmental impacts and social acceptance horizontally across its three pillars, including for geothermal energy.

The topic on geothermal exploration includes, as expected outcomes, increased knowledge to reduce risks of seismicity, as well as an increased engagement of region, city and citizens for geothermal energy.

Other relevant topics under Horizon Europe include solutions for more sustainable geothermal energy, use of geothermal reservoirs for energy storage, advanced exploration technologies and geothermal application in industry.

In addition, the Clean Energy Transition Partnership joint call 2023 includes a specific module on geothermal energy technologies, which targets environmental protection and societal acceptability, notably in the context of improved prospective and exploration techniques.

From the regulatory side, any geothermal project in the EU, whether a public private partnership or not, needs to comply with all relevant planning, permitting, public consultation and environmental rules to ensure all risks are taken into consideration and all concerns are addressed. Newly adopted legislation introduces many new tools to support geothermal energy in the EU.

This includes binding targets for renewable heating and cooling and the promotion of efficient and renewables-based district heating and cooling. It also strengthens energy planning with new local planning requirements for the 1000 largest municipalities in EU and the requirement that district heating systems are taken into account when planning electricity infrastructure.
